title: Why do the fewest presses give place value notation?
description: A question from the book asks why the expressions for the fewest presses also give the Indian place value notation of a number. The video swaps ten presses for one bigger press, shows each count is a single digit, and checks with two numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: ten presses of a button can always be swapped for one press of the next bigger button, so in the fewest way each place holds at most nine presses. Ask the class why ten presses would be wasteful. Watch for students who forget that the biggest button has no bigger neighbour to swap with.

source: Figure it Out, Q3 (why the expression is the place value notation)
video_script.why: The child has seen that ten presses of one button make one press of the next bigger button, and has written numbers as presses of buttons.
video_script.substitution: Ten presses of a button can be swapped for one press of the next bigger button, so each place holds at most nine presses in the fewest way.
video_script.anchor: Why do the expressions for the fewest presses also give the place value notation of the number?
video_script.payoff_line: Each place holds at most nine presses, so the counts are the digits of the number

final_answer.value: Each place holds at most nine presses, so the counts are the digits of the number
final_answer.spoken: each place holds at most nine presses, so the counts are the digits of the number

maths_rules: 10 × 100 = 1 × 1000: ten presses of one button make one press of the next bigger button
in the fewest way no button other than the biggest is pressed ten or more times, since ten presses can be swapped for one
each press count is a single digit from 0 to 9, written in that button's place
video_script.design: One idea: ten presses swap for one bigger press, so each place holds at most nine presses and the counts are the digits. Check with two numbers. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Each button stands for one place: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, and so on.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The press count of a button tells how many of that place we use.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Let us see what the fewest presses do to these counts.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find why the press counts turn out to be the digits.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, look at two neighbouring buttons.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ten presses of the hundred button make the same amount as one press of the thousand button.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 10 presses of a button swap for 1 press of the next bigger button, which uses fewer presses

marks.m1: ten presses of a button are circled
marks.m2: the ten presses are swapped for one bigger press
marks.m3: the biggest button is marked as having no bigger neighbour

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, suppose a button was pressed ten times or more.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We could swap ten of those presses for one press of the next bigger button. That uses fewer presses, so it was not the fewest way.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Only the biggest button has no bigger neighbour to swap with.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: every count is a single digit from 0 to 9; a count of 0 means the button is not pressed; the counts side by side are the digits

marks.m1: each count is boxed as a single digit
marks.m2: the 0 for the hundred button is marked not pressed
marks.m3: the counts are written side by side

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, every other count is then a single digit from zero to nine.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A count of zero means that button is not pressed. The hundred button is not pressed for five thousand seventy two.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Written side by side in order, the counts are the digits of the number.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check: counts 5, 0, 7, 2 side by side make 5072; counts 4, 0, 6, 2, 9 side by side make 40629

marks.m3: the counts 4, 0, 6, 2, 9 are written in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check with five thousand seventy two. The counts are five, zero, seven and two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Side by side they read five thousand seventy two.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Another number, forty thousand six hundred twenty nine, has counts four, zero, six, two and nine.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Side by side they read forty thousand six hundred twenty nine.
